newsitem.title: USA: S&P develops new insurance catastrophe model.
newsitem.headline: S&P develops new insurance catastrophe model.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said it has developed a new model to estimate insurers' exposure to a $20 billion catastrophe.
The new approach also includes a new quantitative framework that assesses the impact catastrophes can have on an insurer's financial strength, as measured by three ratios.
The ratios are compared to benchmarks for the various rating categories, which assists Standard & Poor's in identifying insurers with significant catastrophe exposures.
The new catastrophe exposure model is intended to estimate each insurer's gross exposure to a $20 billion catastrophe.
The output of the model is an aggregate number that represents, at a 95 percent confidence level, Standard & Poor's estimate of an insurer's exposure.
Standard & Poor's emphasizes that the model produces an exposure estimate, not a loss estimate.
"The difference is important," S&P managing director Alan Levin said.
"We are not trying to estimate the amount of loss an insurer could suffer in a given year, but rather the extent of exposure given the insurer's book of business," he said.
Because the output of the model is a gross number, it does not reflect the various alternatives insurers use to cope with their exposures, S&P said.
Those alternatives can be company-specific, industry-wide or a combination of the two.
Company-specific options include reinsurance, alternative sources of liquidity, funding via the capital markets or bank lines, and support from the parent company, S&P said.
Regulatory developments may also help insurers manage their catastrophe exposure.
In California, the California Earthquake Authority is poised to materially reduce an insurer's exposure, while Florida has various residual pool mechanisms to cope with that state's exposure.

S&P said that while it anticipates taking these programs into account when evaluating an insurer's net exposure, full credit may not be given as these programs have not yet been tested by a major catastrophe.
In a report, Standard & Poor's provides the gross catastrophe exposure for the top 20 insurance groups as ranked by year end 1995 statutory surplus, which is the most recent data available, S&P said.
State Farm Mutual Group, which has a triple A claims-paying ability rating, has the largest surplus of the 20 insurers at $25 billion and a gross catastrophe exposure of $5.267 billion.
Allstate Corp's 's Allstate Insurance Co. Group, with a doubleA claims-paying ability rating, has the third highest surplus at $9.4 billion.
It has a gross catastrophe exposure of $3.042 billion.
The output of the new insurer exposure model is viewed as just one tool in Standard & Poor's analysis of an insurer's catastrophe exposure that is then factored into the rating process, S&P said.

"In addition to reviewing the output from the model, our evaluation of an insurer's exposure will continue to involve input from management, as we assess their ability to both quantify and manage their catastrophe exposure," S&P director Kristin Brooks said.
